RagShortTexts: Barcelona's 1258 sea ordinances require a sworn clerk to record contracts and expenses.
Masters must provide fifteen days of food and water, plus two packets of candles.

Variants.Content: Barcelona's maritime commerce depends on accountable obligations and provisions as well as cargo. Section two of the 1258 ordinances requires a trustworthy sworn clerk aged at least twenty on each voyage, keeping an accurate record of expenses. Entries concerning agreements between master and merchants or master and crew require the relevant parties to be present. The clerk cannot predict storms, but provides a written basis for later disputes. Section three requires the master to provide fifteen days of bread, wine, salted meat, vegetables, oil and water, with two packets of candles. Cargo-value thresholds also determine armed overnight attendance by part of the crew and an officer. Mariners swear to protect vessel, equipment, merchants and goods to the best of their ability. Co-owners receiving wages and paid pilots are not exempt from obligations. Other clauses require appropriate merchant consent for specified cargo stowage and entry into places where merchants fear detention. These are particular local ordinances, not identical law in every port. Written records, provisions, watches and consultation jointly sustain a voyage; a wealthy harbour alone does not guarantee safe arrival.

When arranging freight in Barcelona, establish charges, goods and obligations before the clerk. The 1258 ordinances require the relevant parties' presence when agreements are entered, rather than allowing master or merchant to dictate the contract book alone. Fifteen days of supplies are not an afterthought once valuable cargo is aboard: bread, wine, salted meat, vegetables, oil, water and candles appear in the requirements. Merchants risk cargo value while crew undertake navigation and watch duties. Signing an agreement does not mean either party must absorb every conceivable loss.

Aboard a Barcelona merchant ship, understand the oath to protect vessel, equipment and merchandise. Protection does not begin only when an enemy draws alongside. Armed attendance after loading must follow the ordinance, while bread and water determine whether the whole ship can continue. Fifteen days of preparation is a requirement, not a promise of arrival on the fifteenth day. Master and relevant crew must be present before the clerk when their agreement is recorded, providing evidence in later disputes over wages and duties.

Revenue from Barcelona's routes depends on a port order that sustains divided responsibilities. The 1258 ordinances specify sworn clerks, agreements recorded with both parties present, fifteen days of provisions and armed watches after loading. These cannot be reduced to a claim that merchants simply sail at their own risk. Master, merchants and crew have distinct obligations, and certain stowage and entry decisions require merchants' consent. Enforceable agreements help owners assess the cost of a voyage better than unexplained demands for additional service.
